content: Pulled elbow, also known as nursemaid's elbow, is a traumatic condition that occurs exclusively in children under the age of approximately three years. This condition arises due to the unique anatomical characteristics of the developing skeletal system in young children. The forearm consists of two bones: the radius and the ulna. These bones are connected to each other at both the proximal (elbow) and distal (wrist) ends. The forearm is capable of rotational movements known as pronation and supination, which involve rotation around its long axis. During these movements, the ulna remains stationary, as it is connected to the humerus by a simple hinge joint, while the radius rotates, carrying the wrist and hand along with it. To facilitate this rotational movement, the proximal end of the radius is held in close proximity to the ulna by a ligament called the annular ligament. In young children, the proximal end of the radius is conical in shape, with the wider end of the cone situated near the elbow. As the child grows, the shape of the radius changes, becoming more cylindrical, with the proximal end widening further. If the forearm of a young child is subjected to a sudden pulling force, such as when an impatient parent pulls the child’s arm, the traction can cause the radius to be pulled into the annular ligament with sufficient force to become trapped. This results in significant pain, partial limitation of elbow flexion and extension, and a complete loss of pronation and supination in the affected arm. This condition does not occur in adults or older children because the growth-associated changes in the shape of the radius prevent such entrapment. Pulled elbow is a condition that can be effectively treated by a primary care practitioner with minimal skill and complete confidence. To treat the condition, the attending physician must hold the affected arm with one hand just above the elbow and the other hand grasping the child’s hand. While applying compression between these two points, the physician rapidly supinates the forearm. During this maneuver, the physician will feel a distinct click, indicating that the radius has been released from the annular ligament. The child may scream momentarily, and the parent, unless forewarned, may become upset. However, following this procedure, the forearm will regain full function and the child will experience no further pain.
